claims.text: Coupled metadynamics and replica-exchange molecular dynamics will predict high-entropy-alloy melting temperatures within a few kelvin.
The coupled method will predict high-entropy-alloy enthalpies of fusion within a few percent.
The coupled method will accurately predict entropy of fusion.
The coupled method will accurately predict volume changes at melting.
The coupled method will accurately predict liquid-phase thermodynamic properties of high-entropy alloys.
The proposed method will provide predictions efficiently.
Carefully tuned bias potentials, optimized temperature ladders, and selected integration windows will provide adequate thermalization and consistent sampling across diverse alloy compositions.
The enhanced-sampling method overcomes barriers in the complex solid-liquid energy landscape.
The method captures configurational-entropy changes associated with melting.
Coupling metadynamics with replica exchange enables efficient sampling of rare melting-related events.
Efficient rare-event sampling permits reliable estimation of free-energy differences between solid and liquid states.
Reliable solid-liquid free-energy differences enable prediction of melting thermodynamics and associated structural transformations.
Traditional differential scanning calorimetry and standard molecular dynamics show slower convergence or larger deviations for comparable high-entropy-alloy measurements.
The method can satisfy the stated accuracy tolerances across a representative set of high-entropy alloys.
Optimal bias potentials and integration parameters may vary with alloy composition.
The scalability of the method across the full high-entropy-alloy compositional space remains partly untested.

The hypothesis is falsified if predictions for multiple high-entropy-alloy compositions differ from experiments by more than approximately 10 K in melting temperature or 5% in latent heats and other thermodynamic properties.

contradictions.description: The claimed performance is within a few kelvin and a few percent, and the boundary says deviations beyond the specified limits indicate failure, whereas the formal falsification rule uses looser thresholds of about 10 K and 5% and requires failure in multiple compositions. Results can therefore miss the claimed performance without meeting the stated falsification condition.
